name: Wave Function Collapse

lumenary.blurb: Every cell starts as every possible tile. The most constrained cell settles first, and its neighbours must agree, until the whole sheet is one connected drawing.

facts.bestOn: Pictures with a clear mix of light and dark

why: The name comes from quantum mechanics, where something can be in many states until it is measured. Here every cell starts as every possible tile, and the algorithm repeatedly settles the most constrained cell. Because neighbours must agree about the edge they share, one choice forces others, and the whole sheet falls into a consistent drawing without any plan.
how: Treat each tile as a square with a line leaving through any of its four sides, a 4-bit number, so there are 16 tiles.
Apply the one rule: two neighbouring tiles must both have a line through their shared side, or neither. The sheet’s edge is closed.
Start every cell with all 16 possibilities held in a 16-bit mask.
Pick the cell with the fewest tiles left (lowest entropy, plus a little random noise to break ties), then choose one of its tiles with weights from the picture.
Propagate: remove from neighbours any tile that no longer fits, and repeat until all cells are settled.
history: Maxim Gumin published the algorithm in 2016, building on the model synthesis of Paul Merrell (2007) and on texture synthesis research. It spread quickly in game design, where it was used in titles such as Bad North, Caves of Qud and Townscaper to build levels and towns that always make sense.
uses: Procedural levels, maps and towns for games
terms: Here, a measure of how many choices a cell still has.
Passing the consequences of a choice to neighbouring cells.
A number whose binary digits mark which options are possible.
paragraphs: Wave function collapse (Maxim Gumin, 2016) borrows its name and its picture of a superposition from quantum mechanics, but it is a constraint-solving algorithm. Here a tile is a square with a line leaving through any of its four sides (north, east, south, west), a 4-bit number, so there are 16 tiles. The single rule is that two neighbouring tiles must agree on the side they share: either both have a line through it or neither does. The edge of the sheet is closed, so no line leaves the picture. At the start every cell may be any of the 16 tiles, a set held as a 16-bit mask.

The solver picks the cell with the fewest tiles still possible (its lowest entropy, with a little random noise of 0.4 to break ties) and collapses it: one of its remaining tiles is chosen by chance. The chances come from the picture. Each tile k has a weight exp(−(n_k − target)²/1.1), where n_k is the number of line ends on the tile and the target is higher in the heavy, dark parts of the picture and lower in the light, set by the density slider; the empty tile has its weight multiplied by 0.3. The choice is then propagated: neighbours lose the tiles that no longer agree, and so do their neighbours, until nothing more changes. A cell left with no possibility is drawn blank. The tiles are drawn as straight lines, rounded corner arcs or chamfered corners.

equations.note: The next cell to collapse: |D_c| is the number of tiles still possible there, u a random number in [0, 1].
Chance weight of tile k: n_k its line ends, m_k = 0.3 for the empty tile and 1 otherwise, h the heaviness of the picture under the cell, δ the density slider.

equations.note: The adjacency rule on bits: the shared side must either have a line on both tiles or on neither (d + 2 is the opposite side).

presets.text: Chamfered corners give a circuit-board look.
Strong picture control makes dense lines in the dark.
Ink on night paper makes a glowing maze.
